query:
CONTEXT. We make sealed aluminium "cups" as the charge for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic
atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder: induction melting in a graphite crucible with a boron-nitride
wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with argon to ~150-200 mbar, melt at ~800-850 C
pushed by ~0.2 bar argon overpressure through a 0.5-0.7 mm graphite nozzle onto a 40 kHz
sonotrode plate) to make Al-Si powder (target 15-63 um) for laser powder bed fusion and alloy
studies. Today each cup is machined on a lathe from extruded 3/4 in (19 mm) AA 6063-T52 bar:
70 mm long with a 12.7 mm blind bore 57 mm deep (or a 15.9 mm bore and 1.5 mm wall for a
thin-wall version), filled with 6-16 g of gas-atomized AA 4047 (Al-12Si) powder, and closed
by a press-fit 6063 plug with a ~1 mm vent hole (0.013-0.020 mm interference). Three to five
cups (~150-250 g in total) are melted per run. The runs are a Si composition spread (0-30 wt%
4047 powder in 6063) whose composition is computed from the weighed masses, so the cup metal's
own composition and cleanliness matter. The cups exist to put the powder inside bulk metal so
that it melts in contact with liquid, without loose-powder losses and with little oxide
pickup. Current practice: dry or light-oil machining, a 99% IPA flush, and an 80 C dry.

PROPOSAL. To make larger cups (more powder per cup), students are considering sand casting
them instead of machining: melting aluminium (most likely re-melted 6063 offcuts and scrap,
or commercially pure aluminium, or a casting alloy such as A356) in a clay-graphite or SiC
crucible in a university foundry (gas or electric furnace, melting in air, possibly with no
rotary degassing or flux), and hand-pouring into green sand (clay-bonded, ~3-4% moisture) or
chemically bonded no-bake sand moulds with a sand core forming the cavity. The cast cup might
be used as cast, or with only the bore and the plug seat machined.

QUESTION 2 (metal quality after casting, and fitness for this purpose). For the same proposal:
(a) castability of AA 6063 and other wrought 6xxx alloys in sand moulds compared with casting
alloys (A356, 4047 / Al-12Si) and commercially pure Al: fluidity, hot-tearing susceptibility,
shrinkage porosity, freezing range;
(b) as-cast microstructure and properties of sand-cast 6063 or pure Al relative to extruded
6063-T5/T52: grain size, secondary dendrite arm spacing, Mg2Si and beta-AlFeSi intermetallics,
macro- and microsegregation, density, yield strength and ductility;
(c) whether a thin-walled (1.5-3 mm) sand-cast aluminium cup can take a press-fit plug with
0.013-0.020 mm interference without cracking or leaking, given its porosity and lower yield
strength; how gas and shrinkage porosity affect sealing and leak tightness of thin walls;
(d) achievable dimensional tolerances and surface roughness for small sand castings and for
alternatives (gravity permanent-mould casting in graphite or steel, investment casting,
lost-foam), and what machining would still be needed for a press fit;
(e) whether cups cast from re-melted 6063 stay within AA 6063 composition limits (Mg, Fe, Si,
Cu, Zn) and how many remelt cycles it takes to drift out;
(f) other ways to make larger aluminium containers for powder (tube with welded or press-fit
end plugs, impact-extruded or deep-drawn 1xxx/3xxx cans, larger-diameter bar, canning or
compacting powder into a can as in powder-metallurgy HIP canning) and how they compare on
oxide and hydrogen content and on effort.
Give numbers with citations, and say plainly where the evidence is thin or only indirect.
task_summary: Evaluate Sand Casting Versus Machined Aluminium Cups For Powder Charging Including Metallurgical Risks

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier

        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Use the tools to answer the question: CONTEXT. We make sealed aluminium "cups" as the charge for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic
atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder: induction melting in a graphite crucible with a boron-nitride
wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with argon to ~150-200 mbar, melt at ~800-850 C
pushed by ~0.2 bar argon overpressure through a 0.5-0.7 mm graphite nozzle onto a 40 kHz
sonotrode plate) to make Al-Si powder (target 15-63 um) for laser powder bed fusion and alloy
studies. Today each cup is machined on a lathe from extruded 3/4 in (19 mm) AA 6063-T52 bar:
70 mm long with a 12.7 mm blind bore 57 mm deep (or a 15.9 mm bore and 1.5 mm wall for a
thin-wall version), filled with 6-16 g of gas-atomized AA 4047 (Al-12Si) powder, and closed
by a press-fit 6063 plug with a ~1 mm vent hole (0.013-0.020 mm interference). Three to five
cups (~150-250 g in total) are melted per run. The runs are a Si composition spread (0-30 wt%
4047 powder in 6063) whose composition is computed from the weighed masses, so the cup metal's
own composition and cleanliness matter. The cups exist to put the powder inside bulk metal so
that it melts in contact with liquid, without loose-powder losses and with little oxide
pickup. Current practice: dry or light-oil machining, a 99% IPA flush, and an 80 C dry.

PROPOSAL. To make larger cups (more powder per cup), students are considering sand casting
them instead of machining: melting aluminium (most likely re-melted 6063 offcuts and scrap,
or commercially pure aluminium, or a casting alloy such as A356) in a clay-graphite or SiC
crucible in a university foundry (gas or electric furnace, melting in air, possibly with no
rotary degassing or flux), and hand-pouring into green sand (clay-bonded, ~3-4% moisture) or
chemically bonded no-bake sand moulds with a sand core forming the cavity. The cast cup might
be used as cast, or with only the bore and the plug seat machined.

QUESTION 2 (metal quality after casting, and fitness for this purpose). For the same proposal:
(a) castability of AA 6063 and other wrought 6xxx alloys in sand moulds compared with casting
alloys (A356, 4047 / Al-12Si) and commercially pure Al: fluidity, hot-tearing susceptibility,
shrinkage porosity, freezing range;
(b) as-cast microstructure and properties of sand-cast 6063 or pure Al relative to extruded
6063-T5/T52: grain size, secondary dendrite arm spacing, Mg2Si and beta-AlFeSi intermetallics,
macro- and microsegregation, density, yield strength and ductility;
(c) whether a thin-walled (1.5-3 mm) sand-cast aluminium cup can take a press-fit plug with
0.013-0.020 mm interference without cracking or leaking, given its porosity and lower yield
strength; how gas and shrinkage porosity affect sealing and leak tightness of thin walls;
(d) achievable dimensional tolerances and surface roughness for small sand castings and for
alternatives (gravity permanent-mould casting in graphite or steel, investment casting,
lost-foam), and what machining would still be needed for a press fit;
(e) whether cups cast from re-melted 6063 stay within AA 6063 composition limits (Mg, Fe, Si,
Cu, Zn) and how many remelt cycles it takes to drift out;
(f) other ways to make larger aluminium containers for powder (tube with welded or press-fit
end plugs, impact-extruded or deep-drawn 1xxx/3xxx cans, larger-diameter bar, canning or
compacting powder into a can as in powder-metallurgy HIP canning) and how they compare on
oxide and hydrogen content and on effort.
Give numbers with citations, and say plainly where the evidence is thin or only indirect.

    author = "Fracchia, Elisa and Gobber, Federico Simone and Rosso, Mario",
    title = "Effects of Casting-Additives on the Microstructure Evolution of Hypoeutectic Aluminium-Silicon Alloys",
    year = "2020",

Abstract:
Since the industries are called to produce environmentally friendly products, the research is moving toward new improved materials. In this panorama, aluminium alloys find applications for a large range of products. In the automotive, as well as in the aerospace, sector, aluminium alloys are largely adopted, thanks to their high specific properties and their light weight. Moreover, common casting techniques permit us to realize complex high-quality components. These components may be realized by using casting techniques adopting casting-additives, such as modifiers or refiners. In this work, the effect of refining and modification was studied in terms of microstructural evolution of the intermetallic phases in two aluminium-silicon alloys (EN AC 45300 and EN AC 43500). Microstructures were analyzed through micro-hardness measures, and we found a reduction in the standard deviation of the hardness with the addition of additives. Furthermore, secondary dendrites arms spacings (SDAS) were measured, evidencing a decrease in SDAS by adding casting additives. A strong correlation was found between the adding of additives and the possibility of containing the size of the silicon and of all the intermetallic phases opening up to the possibility of tailoring the microstructures.

Abstract:
<jats:p>To meet aero-engine aluminum skirt requirements, an experiment was carried out using Al–Nb–B2O3–CuO as the reaction system and a 6063 aluminum alloy melt as the reaction medium for a contact reaction, and 6063 aluminum matrix composites containing in situ particles were prepared with the near-liquid-phase line-casting method after the reaction was completed. The effects of the reactant molar ratio and the preheating temperature on the in situ reaction process and products were explored in order to determine the influence of in situ-reaction-product features on the organization and the qualities of the composites. Thermodynamic calculations, DSC analysis, and experiments revealed that the reaction could continue when the molar ratio of the reactants of Al–Nb–B2O3–CuO was 6:1:1:1.5. A kinetic study revealed that the Al thermal reaction in the system produced Al2O3 and [B], and the [B] atoms interacted with Nb to generate NbB2. With increasing temperature, the interaction between the Nb and the AlB2 produced hexagonal NbB2 particles with an average longitudinal size of 1 μm and subspherical Al2O3 particles with an average longitudinal size of 0.2 μm. The microstructure of the composites was reasonably fine, with an estimated equiaxed crystal size of around 22 μm, a tensile strength of 170 MPa, a yield strength of 135 MPa, an elongation of 13.4%, and a fracture energy of 17.05 × 105 KJ/m3, with a content of 2.3 wt% complex-phase particles. When compared to the matrix alloy without addition, the NbB2 and Al2O3 particles produced by the in situ reaction had a significant refinement effect on the microstructure of the alloy, and the plasticity of the composite in the as-cast state was improved while maintaining higher strength and better overall mechanical properties, allowing for industrial mass production.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The effect of the application of forced convection during the continuous solidification of A356 aluminum alloy over microstructural parameters of AlFeSi phases has been presented in this work. The investigation has been made on the fact that as an alloy solidifies under the action of a rotating magnetic field; a non-dendritic casting structure will be obtained. The Al-Si alloy has been studied using magnetic stirring equipment with permanent magnets. This device has allowed the study of the rotational speed (degree of stirring) effect on the micro- and macro- solidification structure. Different analyses and tests have been carried out, such as micro- and mac -ro-structural analysis. The results have shown that magnetic stirring affects the cooling curves, expanding the solidification range. Microstructural evolution of the alloys has also been observed, from a 100% dendritic structure to a mature rosette type structure, in addition to a notable grain size decrease, which may improve the materi al’s mechanical behavior. The results show that all the microstructural parameters of the AlFeSi phases (quan -tity, size, shape factor, particle area, and aspect ratio) decrease when stirring is applied to the alloy during its solidification.

Comparative study of FSW and TIG welding of AA3003 aluminium flange joints under varying tool geometries and rotational speeds Valid Text Names: 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 1-2', 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 2-5', 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 5-9', 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 9-14', 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 14-16', 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 16-17', 'sabry2026comparativestudyof pages 17-18' BibTex: @article{sabry2026comparativestudyof, author = "Sabry, Ibrahim and El-Zathry, Noah E. and Mahamood, Rasheedat M. and Akinlabi, Stephen and Woo, Wai Lok", title = "Comparative study of FSW and TIG welding of AA3003 aluminium flange joints under varying tool geometries and rotational speeds", year = "2026", journal = "Welding in the World", volume = "70", pages = "763-780", month = "Jan", doi = "10.1007/s40194-026-02352-y", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s40194-026-02352-y", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "3", issn = "0043-2288" } Abstract: Abstract Flange joints are widely used in pipelines, heat exchangers, and pressure-retaining aluminium structures, yet their behaviour under friction stir welding (FSW) remains insufficiently explored in the literature. This study addresses this gap by evaluating the combined effects of tool geometry and rotational speed on the microstructural and mechanical performance of FSW AA3003 flange joints, with Tungsten Inert Gas (TIG) welding used as a benchmark. The conical-pin tool produced superior weld quality, generating refined stir-zone grains (7.26 µm), higher hardness (46 HV₀.₂), and the highest tensile strength (185 MPa) owing to enhanced material flow and dynamic recrystallisation. The cylindrical pin yielded slightly lower properties (44 HV₀.₂, 165 MPa), while TIG welds exhibited coarse dendritic structures and reduced strength. Hydrostatic testing further demonstrated the sealing advantage of FSW, with conical-pin welds remaining leak-tight up to 32 bar, compared with failure at 23–25 bar in TIG joints. Ceramic shells used in investment casting must be sufficiently permeable to allow cavity gases to escape during pouring; inadequate venting produces gas porosity, cold shuts and misruns. Standard practice (JB/T 4153 − 2025; HB 5352.4–2004) determines permeability on an idealised "ping-pong ball" specimen, whereas the wall that governs filling is built on clusters whose faces are coated in different orientations. The permeability of a mullite-based shell system (colloidal silica binder, 7.5-layer product build) was therefore measured directly on the shell body at 25°C and 50% relative humidity over 1–5 kPa gauge. Nine body samples taken from a production bent-pipe casting mould (upper-side, lower-side and bottom faces; three sampling points each) were tested after a 200°C/30 min firing treatment, with two standard ball specimens in parallel as the benchmark. The shell body yielded a permeability coefficient K of 16.93 ± 0.69 (upper-side), 17.18 ± 1.44 (lower-side) and 11.37 ± 1.05 m⁴·N⁻¹·min⁻¹ (bottom); the bottom face was 33%–34% less permeable, reflecting gravity-driven slurry pooling, stucco shadowing and seal-coat accumulation on downward-facing surfaces. K was effectively pressure-independent, and within-point repeatability (coefficient of variation ≤ 3.7%) approached that of the ball specimens. Direction-resolved body measurement thus yields production-representative values where the ball specimen cannot. Presented as a methodological pilot, the work proposes a provisional qualification protocol: fixed sampling on the three faces at a single 3 kPa pressure, with statistical control limits to be consolidated as further moulds are sampled.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Increasing the post-consumer recycled content (PCRC) of aluminum automotive body sheet (ABS) is a promising pathway to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ABS production. However, progress is constrained by the limited end-of-life vehicle (ELV) ABS scrap available and the compositional mismatches between contaminated scrap streams and alloy specifications. This study identifies cross ABS life cycle strategies that sheet mills, automotive OEMs, and recyclers can implement and quantifies their effects using a composition-specific dynamic material flow analysis to model sheet demand and scrap availability coupled with a linear optimization framework that determines annual PCRC potential under product-demand, scrap-supply, and alloy-composition constraints. A supply chain emissions model links PCRC gains to GHG reductions. By 2050, ABS scrap from U.S. ELVs could supply up to 33% of the ABS ingot demand needed to meet U.S. requirements for ABS components, yet PCRC remains negligible under business-as-usual (BAU) strategies due to compositional incompatibilities. Effective strategies to increase the PCRC include: (1) sheet mills developing high-residual-content (HRC) “recycle-friendly” alloys; (2) OEMs shifting 5xxx-series component designs to 6xxx alloys; and (3) recyclers either extracting sheet-rich sub-assemblies before shredding or adopting advanced sorting technologies to separate shredded ELV aluminum scrap by alloy series. Achieving a PCRC that approaches the physical maximum (33%) occurs only when multiple stakeholders act to implement complementary strategies. The combination of ELV scrap sorting by alloy series and deployment of HRC alloys is particularly effective. Together, these measures could raise PCRC to 28% by 2050, increase total scrap content (including production scrap) to 76%, and cut annual ABS component supply chain emissions by up to 42%.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p> The annual generation of industrial solid waste has exceeded 10 billion metric tons, and its resource recovery poses a major challenge to global sustainable development. This paper reviews research progress on the preparation of ceramic-metal composites using typical industrial wastes—such as red mud, fly ash, coal gangue, zinc furnace slag, waste refractory materials, recycled aluminum, and aluminum ash—as raw materials through processes including high-temperature sintering, carbon thermal reduction, and hot-press forging. It reveals common patterns across different waste-to-material conversion pathways: (1) “harmful components” in the waste can be redefined as “functional components”; (2) the low-melting-point aluminosilicate liquid phase plays a dual role as both a reaction medium and an interfacial binder in all high-temperature systems, and its viscosity-temperature relationship directly determines the pore structure and interfacial bonding strength; (3) Dispersion strengthening and grain boundary pinning of the reinforcing phase are universal mechanisms for enhancing hardness and strength; however, an increase in the ceramic phase is typically accompanied by a decrease in elongation. Nevertheless, all systems face common bottlenecks: energy consumption at each stage has not been quantitatively assessed over the entire life cycle; there is a lack of systematic research on how fluctuations in raw material composition affect product consistency; and a scale-up pathway from batch laboratory operations to continuous industrial production has yet to be established.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p><p dir="ltr">Lightweighting is in the spotlight of innovations in the automotive industry owing to the demand of energy-efficient electric and hybrid vehicles. Lightweight aluminum (Al) alloys have been leading this global industrial trend as the primary materials for the structural components of vehicles. Due to the advancement in technologies, Al alloys can be fabricated via novel techniques that can improve certain traits like superior strength-ductility synergy in the same range as that of structural steels. As these industries grow, there is an impending need to tailor the alloy microstructures with a proper control of the process parameters like solidification thermodynamics and kinetics, along with the alloy chemistry. This dissertation begins with the primary goal to understand the deformation behavior of a newly-developed low-iron containing, vacuum-assisted high pressure die-cast aluminum-silicon alloy, commercially named Silafont®-36 alloy under static and cyclic loading conditions. Throughout the several investigations in this work, it was observed that the presence of a heterogeneous microstructure led to increased tensile and compressive strength, and elastic modulus than several other commercial Al-Si cast alloys. The cast alloy showed improved ductility owing to its uniquely modified eutectic structure. Load-bearing ability of the eutectic Si particles, dislocations generated due to thermal mismatch between Al matrix and Si particles, and Orowan looping were found to be the predominant strengthening mechanisms in the cast alloy. The alloy showed improved fatigue resistance and a strong cyclic hardening effect in the cast form. Upon solutionizing and overaging treatments of the cast alloy, changes in the microstructure significantly altered the static and cyclic deformation behavior. A novel method was proposed to evaluate the intrinsic fatigue toughness of the alloy in different conditions, which was established as a material constant. This further served as an important parameter to more accurately predict fatigue life of the alloy in cast and heat-treated conditions. In a nutshell, this work constituted an informative benchmark for unravelling the mysteries of the macro-, meso-, and micro-scale deformation behavior that led to improved mechanical performance of a lightweight automotive-grade Al-Si alloy.</p></jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>A356 aluminum alloy has been widely applied in the automotive, aerospace, and marine industries thanks to a combination of superior mechanical properties, namely lightweight, high corrosion resistance, and adequate mechanical strength. However, aluminum casting often produces defects such as porosity, misruns, and shrinkage, which significantly degrade the final product's quality and integrity. This study examines how variations in casting parameters and duct system design affect the quality of A356 aluminum tensile test specimens according to the JIS H 5202 standard, using Altair Inspire Cast simulation software. The simulation varied casting temperature, molten-metal flow rate, and duct-system geometry to observe mold filling, solidification, and defect formation. The simulation results show that optimizing these three parameters significantly reduces internal defects and produces a more even solidification distribution. The optimal configuration was a casting temperature of 720°C, a flow rate of 0.45 m/s, and a tapered ducted bottom gating system design, which Inspire Cast analysis predicted would yield the lowest porosity index (<0.5%). The tensile test specimens are printed using optimal parameters and physically tested according to the JIS H 5202 standard. The mechanical test results showed an average tensile strength of 215 MPa, yield strength of 165 MPa, and elongation of 5.8%. These values meet or exceed the minimum limits required by JIS H 5202: UTS = 195 MPa, yield strength = 130 MPa, and elongation = 4%. Metallographic observations using optical microscopy also confirmed the lack of porosity in the optimal specimen compared with the control specimen, with the specimen density reaching 2.67 g/cm³, close to the theoretical value for alloy A356.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000004

From text 'campbell2000theconceptof pages 6-8'.

J. Campbell. The concept of net shape for castings. Materials & Design, 21:373-380, Aug 2000. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0261-3069(99)00072-2, doi:10.1016/s0261-3069(99)00072-2. This article has 88 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides dimensional variability information, but it does not give surface-roughness (Ra) values for aluminium sand castings, permanent-mould/gravity-die castings, or investment castings. For a good aluminium sand-casting process, the stated probable variability is about ±0.04% of casting length; for a 1 m casting this corresponds to approximately ±0.40 mm. The stated best-case potential error is ±0.10% of length plus ±0.25 mm independent of length, giving approximately ±1.25 mm total variability for a 1 m casting. The article identifies high-technology sand casting and pressure die casting as having the best dimensional reproducibility. Permanent-mould casting is represented by gravity-die casting in the excerpt and is less accurate than precision/high-technology sand casting; for a 500 mm aluminium casting, changing from gravity die to precision sand is predicted to improve accuracy by a factor of roughly 2 to 4. Production measurements cited for cylinder heads found accurate sand castings to be more than twice as accurate as standard gravity-die castings. Investment (lost-wax) casting is accurate for small components, but its dimensional variability increases with casting size and can become comparable to low-technology sand casting for large castings. The excerpt does not establish standard achievable tolerances or Ra ranges for each process.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this study, the effect of three different levels of iron impurity on the grain structure and texture of a fibrous AA6110 alloy after hot extrusion was investigated. Microstructural examination was carried out to measure the microtexture and the results were correlated with tensile and bending mechanical properties. Results demonstrated that the fragmented intermetallic particles after extrusion stimulate the nucleation of new grains, therefore refining the grain structure. The thickness of peripheral coarse grains was found to decrease by increasing Fe content due to increasing nano-sized dispersoid precipitation density. Increment Fe-rich intermetallics on the one hand leads to entrapment of Si solute reducing free Si needed for precipitation hardening shown via thermodynamic calculations. The bending formability was found to correlate with the grain structure of the PCG thickness. The results are compared with Part 1 of this research on the study of Fe content in recrystallized alloys. This work helps to a better understanding of recyclability in Al extrusion alloys.</jats:p>

The deep microstructural observation from macro to nanosized particles show the grain structure, particle stimulated nucleation, and dispersoid precipitation. Additional Fe in the composition of alloys result in increment of Fe-based intermetallic phase which break down and stretch during extrusion while grain structure evolves by dynamic recrystallization.</jats:p>

Abstract:
For aluminium alloys, precipitation strengthening is controlled by age-hardening heat treatments, including solution treatment, quenching, and ageing. In terms of technological applications, quenching is considered a critical step, because detrimental quench-induced precipitation must be avoided to exploit the full age-hardening potential of the alloy. The alloy therefore needs to be quenched faster than a critical cooling rate, but slow enough to avoid undesired distortion and residual stresses. These contrary requirements for quenching can only be aligned based on detailed knowledge of the kinetics of quench-induced precipitation. Until the beginning of the 21st century, the kinetics of relevant solid-solid phase transformations in aluminium alloys could only be estimated by ex-situ testing of different properties. Over the past ten years, significant progress has been achieved in this field of materials science, enabled by the development of highly sensitive differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) techniques. This review presents a comprehensive report on the solid-solid phase transformation kinetics in Al alloys covering precipitation and dissolution reactions during heating from different initial states, dissolution during solution annealing and to a vast extent quench-induced precipitation during continuous cooling over a dynamic cooling rate range of ten orders of magnitude. The kinetic analyses are complemented by sophisticated micro- and nano-structural analyses and continuous cooling precipitation (CCP) diagrams are derived. The measurement of enthalpies released by quench-induced precipitation as a function of the cooling rate also enables predictions of the quench sensitivities of Al alloys using physically-based models. Various alloys are compared, and general aspects of quench-induced precipitation in Al alloys are derived.

    year = "2020",

    issn = "1939-5981"
}


Abstract:
In order to produce cast components, which meet the quality requirements of the automotive and aerospace industries, the control of liquid metal quality prior to the casting process is essential. Rotary degassing is the most commonly used melt treatment method in the foundry industry, which can effectively reduce the inclusion and solute hydrogen content of the metal. This procedure is often combined with fluxing, which allows more efficient inclusion removal during melt processing. In this study, the effects of rotary degassing treatments executed with and without flux addition on the melt cleanliness were compared. The quality of the molten metal was characterized by the microscopic inspection of K -mold specimens, X-ray computed tomography of reduced pressure test samples, and by Density-Index evaluation. The inclusions found on the fracture surfaces of K -mold samples were analyzed with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Based on the results, rotary degassing coupled with flux addition can be an effective inclusion and solute hydrogen removal technique that can significantly improve melt quality. On the other hand, rotary degassing executed without flux addition can increase the inclusion content of the melts. This can be attributed to the chemical reaction between the liquid alloy and the N 2 purging gas during the degassing process. It was also found that inclusion content highly influences the tendency to porosity formation.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'mckenna2010gravityandcentrifugal pages 131-137'.

N McKenna. Gravity and centrifugal casting of light metal alloys using rapidly produced sand moulds. Unknown journal, 2010.

The excerpt does not provide a numerical hydrogen content for aluminium castings poured in sand moulds without degassing, nor does it give numerical hydrogen-solubility values for liquid and solid aluminium. It explains that hydrogen dissolves in molten aluminium and that the liquid-to-solid phase change causes a dramatic reduction in solubility. During solidification, the impinging dendritic network traps the rejected gas, producing hydrogen-related microporosity and macroporosity. The un-degassed specimens shown in Figure 3.32 were used to verify hydrogen porosity. The text distinguishes gas porosity from shrinkage porosity, while noting that hydrogen porosity can add to pre-existing shrinkage porosity. It also states that hydrogen porosity depends on solidification time: rapid cooling suppresses interdendritic porosity and limits hydrogen transfer into the liquid, whereas slow cooling promotes interdendritically distributed hydrogen-containing voids. Hydrogen solubility is described as dependent on the partial pressure of hydrogen in the atmosphere, represented by the excerpt’s equation (3.3), although the equation’s formatting is incomplete in the supplied text. Thus, the passage supports a qualitative liquid-versus-solid explanation but not specific hydrogen concentration or solubility numbers.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 20-23'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt provides a qualitative explanation of hydrogen-related porosity in aluminium castings, but it does not state a numerical hydrogen content for castings poured into sand moulds without degassing. Hydrogen has substantially greater solubility in liquid aluminium than in solid aluminium. During solidification, the decreasing solubility causes dissolved hydrogen to be rejected from solution; if it cannot escape, it can form gas porosity within the casting. The text identifies hydrogen absorption during melting as an important interaction between the aluminium melt and its environment. It also emphasizes that melt handling and previous pouring operations can introduce defects, while careful, quiescent handling during final casting can reduce further defect formation. The excerpt discusses sand casting as a versatile and economical process, but it does not provide a specific hydrogen-solubility value, porosity percentage, or measured gas content for sand-mould castings produced without degassing. Numerical values would therefore need to come from the subsequent section on hydrogen dissolution or from another source dealing specifically with melt hydrogen measurement and porosity in untreated sand castings.

## pqac-00000020

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 35-39'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt does not provide a numerical hydrogen content for aluminium castings poured in sand moulds without degassing, nor does it state a specific numerical solubility value for hydrogen in liquid and solid aluminium. It does establish the relevant qualitative relationship: hydrogen solubility is greater in liquid aluminium and low in solid aluminium. During solidification, hydrogen is rejected from the solid solution and diffuses into bifilms, where it enlarges cavities and produces gas porosity. The initial hydrogen concentration strongly controls the result: low concentrations produce pores later in solidification and generally yield smaller pores, whereas high concentrations cause earlier formation and substantially larger pores. The passage also indicates that faster cooling or solidification reduces the time available for hydrogen diffusion and therefore decreases porosity. Sand moulds and the absence of degassing are not specifically quantified in this excerpt; consequently, a numerical hydrogen concentration or porosity percentage for that casting condition cannot be inferred from the supplied text. Additional data or a cited table/figure from the source would be needed for those values.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 23-27'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt does not provide numerical values for hydrogen content or porosity in aluminium castings poured into sand moulds without degassing. It explains that hydrogen enters the melt primarily through the dissociation of water vapour; moisture may come from fluxes, crucibles, refractories, charge materials, and humid atmospheric conditions. The cited reaction is 2 Al + 3 H2O → Al2O3 + 3 H2, followed by hydrogen entering solution in aluminium. Hydrogen solubility is high in liquid aluminium and decreases as temperature falls. The solubility is substantially lower in solid aluminium, so hydrogen rejected during solidification may precipitate as gas and generate porosity. If conditions do not allow precipitation, the hydrogen can remain dissolved in a supersaturated state. Thus, without degassing, the likely consequences are elevated dissolved hydrogen and increased porosity risk, but the excerpt supplies neither the actual hydrogen concentration nor a measured porosity percentage for sand-mould castings. Quantitative values would need to come from the referenced Figure 2.2, Figure 2.3, or another source specifically addressing un-degassed sand casting.

The excerpt does not provide a specific measured hydrogen content or porosity value for aluminium castings poured in sand moulds without degassing. It reports that the A356 experiments used hydrogen levels of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 mL/100 g Al, designated low, mid, and high, respectively. The study cast tensile bars in sand moulds, but the provided pages describe the experimental design rather than results for an untreated, non-degassed melt. Conceptually, hydrogen is more soluble in liquid aluminium than in solid aluminium, and its solubility decreases as the metal cools. During solidification, growing dendrites reject hydrogen, which can contribute to porosity. However, the authors emphasize that hydrogen alone is not sufficient to explain pore formation: oxide biﬁlms provide sites that aid pore nucleation and growth. They also report that turbulence and vortex formation during rotary degassing can increase the biﬁlm population and may affect porosity and mechanical properties more strongly than hydrogen content itself. Therefore, this excerpt supports the qualitative liquid-versus-solid solubility relationship and gives the tested hydrogen ranges, but it does not establish the requested no-degassing hydrogen/porosity result or numerical solubility values.

## pqac-00000023

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 74-78'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt does not give a specific hydrogen concentration or porosity value for aluminium castings poured in sand moulds without degassing. It does provide a relevant approximate reference: results in several figures show a cutoff at about 1.0 mL/kg Al, below which pore formation may not be observed or may be strongly limited. The text cautions that porosity cannot be attributed to dissolved hydrogen alone. In reduced-pressure testing, gas originating as air entrained in oxide bifilms can contribute substantially to pore formation, especially when the data fall below the theoretical hydrogen–density relationship. The proposed mechanism is that bifilms provide pre-existing voids into which dissolved hydrogen diffuses; pore formation is therefore described primarily as a growth process rather than homogeneous nucleation. Regarding solubility, the excerpt states qualitatively that hydrogen has high solubility in both liquid and solid aluminium and high diffusivity, but it does not provide numerical solubility values for either phase or a liquid-to-solid solubility ratio. It also notes that solid solubility depends on cooling rate and alloying elements. Numerical sand-mould, no-degassing data and phase-specific hydrogen-solubility values would therefore need to be obtained from other pages or sources.

Influence of Intermetallic Phases and Grain Refinement on Hot-Tearing Susceptibility in 6xxx-Series Aluminum Alloys Valid Text Names: 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 1-2', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 2-4', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 4-6', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 6-8', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 8-11', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 11-13', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 13-14', 'giansante2026influenceofintermetallic pages 14-14' BibTex: @article{giansante2026influenceofintermetallic, author = "Giansante, Emidio and Fabrizi, Alberto and Timelli, Giulio", title = "Influence of Intermetallic Phases and Grain Refinement on Hot-Tearing Susceptibility in 6xxx-Series Aluminum Alloys", year = "2026", journal = "International Journal of Metalcasting", month = "Aug", doi = "10.1007/s40962-026-02098-9", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s40962-026-02098-9", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issn = "1939-5981" } Abstract: Abstract The hot-tearing susceptibility (HTS) of three experimental 6XXX-series Al alloys with controlled variations in Si, Mg, Fe, and Mn content was investigated using constrained rod casting (CRC) tests, and the effect of an Al–Ti–B grain-refining agent was also evaluated. CRC test results validated the hot-tearing indices predicted by Kou’s criterion, demonstrating strong agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental observations. Microstructural observations and fracture-surface analyses revealed that the presence of the Al 15 (Fe,Mn) 3 Si 2 phase with Chinese-script morphology contributes to the formation of a strong solid skeleton in the α -Al matrix, enhancing hot-tearing resistance. In contrast, the β -Al 5 FeSi phase, exhibiting a plate-like morphology, acts as a stress concentrator and disrupts interdendritic feeding, promoting hot-tear initiation. The influence of adding a Ti-based grain refiner was also evaluated, as grain refinement generally reduces hot-tear propagation along intergranular voids. However, because the alloys already exhibited a fine as-cast microstructure in the CRC castings, further grain refinement yielded only a marginal decrease in hot-tearing resistance. These implications provide important insights for optimizing alloy design and process parameters, improving the structural integrity of aluminum castings for industrial applications and supporting the use of recycled feedstocks in industrial applications. Evaluation of the Enhanced Constrained Rod Casting Test for Hot Tearing of 7xxx Aluminium Alloys Valid Text Names: 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 1-6', 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 6-11', 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 11-15', 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 15-22', 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 22-27', 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 27-31', 'gong2026evaluationofthe pages 31-33' BibTex: @article{gong2026evaluationofthe, author = "Gong, Zheng and Yu, Qing and Wen, Lianjian and Peng, Mingjun and Yao, Jianjun and Yang, Hongmei and Li, Mengnie", title = "Evaluation of the Enhanced Constrained Rod Casting Test for Hot Tearing of 7xxx Aluminium Alloys", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10401599/v1", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10401599/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", year = "2026", month = "Aug", journal = "Unknown journal" } Abstract: Abstract

The enhanced constrained rod casting (ECRC) test has been validated mainly on narrow-freezing-range alloys such as A206 and A380, and its repeatability and interpretation for wide-freezing-range 7xxx Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloys remain largely unreported. Here, four cast 7xxx alloys containing 0.081–0.232 wt.% Fe were used as a case series, with three independent ECRC trials per composition. Crack widths, fracture locations, contraction load and temperature were cross-examined against JMatPro–Kou calculations, backscattered-electron/energy-dispersive spectroscopy (BSE/EDS) quantification and elastic–viscoplastic numerical simulations. Fracture locations were highly repeatable—the column-end junctions of the short rods A and B fractured in all twelve castings (100%)—whereas the long-rod (C, D) fractures were dispersed. The all-rod hot-tearing susceptibility (HTS) gave means of 67.1 ± 6.7, 74.1 ± 3.8, 68.3 ± 7.9 and 62.7 ± 19.0 for the Base, #1, #2 and #3 alloys; the between-alloy differences were smaller than the casting-to-casting variability and not statistically significant (p = 0.730). The peak contraction load was far more repeatable and ranked alloy #1 highest (87.2 ± 3.2 N, p = 0.077), as did the Kou index of the measured compositions, whereas a Fe-only scan produced nearly invariant indices—showing that the differences originate from the multicomponent solidification path, not from Fe alone. The simulation reproduced the longest late-mushy-stage residence and highest accumulated plastic strain at the A/B junctions, matching the 100% fracture frequency; rods C and D solidified first at mid-length, cutting off feeding and making their response geometry-dominated. The ECRC test is thus applicable to 7xxx alloys provided that short-rod and long-rod responses are interpreted separately, and that fracture-location statistics and the load signal—rather than the crack-width score—are used as the evaluation metrics.

Abstract:
This study explores the potential of aluminum wine bottles as a sustainable alternative to traditional glass bottles, emphasizing their recyclability and environmental advantages. It reviews the potential use of Al-Mn-Mg 3xxx alloys in beverage can bodies and examines various applications of aluminum containers in packaging, including recyclable beverage containers. The manufacturing processes for aluminum bottles, including casting, rolling, punching, and deformation techniques, are discussed in detail, with a particular focus on their impact on mechanical properties and microstructure. The preference for 1xxx aluminum alloys in impact extrusion is explained, highlighting their lower flow stress and higher formability compared to 3xxx alloys, and the microstructural changes induced by various processing steps are analyzed. Challenges related to using recycled aluminum and their effects on mechanical properties and microstructure during aluminum bottle production are also addressed. One objective is to increase the proportion of recycled alloyed material used in aluminum bottle manufacturing. Depending on the technique employed, the fraction of alloyed recycled material can vary. The percentage of recycled alloyed material (3xxx series Al alloys) in cold backward impact extrusion could be raised by 60%. High-speed blow forming could facilitate the production of aluminum bottles with a recycled alloyed material ranging from 50 to 100% of the 3xxx series aluminum can body alloys. The high-speed drawing and ironing (DWI) process can produce large-format aluminum bottles (up to 750 mL), utilizing at least 90% of the recycled 3xxx series can body stock. Furthermore, the paper discusses the importance of optimized heat treatment designs in enhancing mechanical properties and controlling microstructural evolution in alloyed aluminum materials, such as 3xxx series alloys. The study concludes with a need for further research to deepen our understanding of the metallurgical aspects of aluminum bottle manufacturing and to optimize the use of recycled aluminum in packaging solutions, with a specific focus on improving mechanical properties and microstructural integrity. This comprehensive review aims to contribute to the development of more sustainable packaging practices in the beverage industry by providing insights into the interplay between manufacturing processes, mechanical properties, and microstructure of aluminum bottles.

Abstract:
Pressure tightness is important for many die-cast aluminium castings, but the interconnected porosity formed in the aluminium alloy high-pressure die castings (HPDC) can form a network connecting several surfaces of the casting, especially as a result of machining after casting. The resulting potential leakage path can be imagined as a series of discontinuities varying in size over wide limits, where voids of different volumes are connected by channels of smaller cross section. Although vacuum impregnation is often used to ensure pressure-tightness is a robust technology, cavity systems through the casting can still cause leakage after impregnation. This study addresses the issues of the impregnation of discontinuities with a complex geometry. The elementary part of a complex cavity geometry consists of a cavity and a capillary channel. We estimated the limited permeability of the capillary section using a mathematical model based on the Hagen–Poiseuille equation. The calculation results prove that the degree of filling of the cavity with a capillary section is basically a function of the geometrical characteristics of the cavity, primarily the radius of the capillary. If the cavity system also contains a section with a diameter of less than 28 μm, impregnation does not necessarily ensure the gas tightness of the casting. Depending on the radius of the capillary, the impregnation of a cavity of a given volume and connected to the surface through a capillary section of a given length can produce three different results. Above a certain capillary radius, filling is complete, below a certain capillary radius only the capillary itself will contain resin, and between the two limit values, the partial impregnation of the cavity is expected but the capillary section is not filled.

Abstract:
The porosity of die-cast aluminum alloys is a determining factor for the quality of the product. In this paper, we studied the porosity of a selected part of a die-cast AlSi9Cu3(Fe) compressor part by computer tomography and metallography. In the case of this part, the achievable resolution by CT, a non-destructive testing method, was 30 μm—this method could not detect smaller cavities. Based on metallographic analysis, the percentage of defects larger than 30 μm ranges from 10 to 30% of the total number of defects, which represents 75–95% of the defective area (area ratio). Impregnation with methacrylate resin (used to seal cavities to prevent leakage) can be detected with UV-illuminated optical microscopic examination on metallographically prepared specimens. As confirmed by scanning electron microscopy, partial filling and partial impregnation can occur in a system of shrinkage cavities.

Abstract:
Company SAG (Salzburger Aluminium AG) is a supplier of fuel tanks, LNG and hydraulic tanks, air reservoirs and structural applications for the commercial vehicle and automotive industry. The company’s expertise is welding but SAG also has a 25 years history in Semi-Solid casting starting in 1993 when the first Thixocasting cell was installed in Lend/Austria. Since then SAG is participating on the diverse casting market and competes with other processes looking for applications for which Semi-Solid processing has a unique selling proposition. This contribution gives examples of industrialized components and will outline their significant characteristics and advantages in comparison to conventional casting processes. Furthermore the development of Semi-Solid cast components, the production process chain as well as commercial aspects will be outlined. The bottom line is that usually it is not a single advantage of Semi-Solid casting that will make a product attractive for the customer but a combination of several of them. Moreover it is not just the casting process itself but the efficiency of the whole production process chain that will result in a commercially successful product.

Abstract:
In this paper, the results of computed tomography and destructive testing of a die cast, gas tight aluminium part are compared and analysed with the aim of refining the porosity map. The mapping of the continuity defects detected by the two methods makes it possible to estimate the number, shape and distribution of continuity defects on and in the immediate vicinity of the machined surface, and to compare the characteristics of continuity defects detected by non-destructive and sequential fine machining. Based on the results of the CT scan of a given casting, we also performed destructive testing to find defects in a selected part of the casting by sequential fine machining. The basic criterion for the choice of the cutting parameters was to minimize the plastic deformation (smearing) on the machined surface, i.e. to clearly identify porosity. We then investigated the position, shape and other characteristics of porosity on the surfaces. The results and differences resulting from the two different methods are also analysed.

The excerpt indicates that cast 6xxx-series Al–Mg–Si alloys have a measurable susceptibility to hot tearing during the final stages of solidification, when interdendritic separation and solid feeding occur. Hot-tearing susceptibility is controlled by composition, feeding behavior, thermal and mechanical stresses, grain size, and the type, size, and distribution of intermetallic phases. Increasing solute content does not produce a simple monotonic response; susceptibility may follow a K(lambda)-shaped trend, initially increasing to a peak and then decreasing at higher concentrations. One cited result places peak susceptibility at approximately 0.10–0.25 wt.% Si and 0.1–0.2 wt.% Mg, although hot tearing can also occur at higher solute levels. Magnesium increases may improve resistance through greater Mg2Si formation. Iron-bearing phases have contrasting effects: plate-like or needle-like beta-Al5FeSi impedes interdendritic liquid feeding and promotes crack initiation, whereas Chinese-script alpha-Al15(Fe,Mn)3Si2 strengthens the solid skeleton and improves resistance; manganese can promote transformation of beta-Fe into alpha-Fe. The excerpt does not provide freezing-range, fluidity, or comparative numerical data for 6063, A356, and Al–12Si alloys.

The excerpt indicates that porous aluminium castings can sometimes be made pressure-tight or leak-tight, but success depends strongly on the geometry and connectivity of the porosity rather than simply on total porosity volume. Leakage occurs through interconnected cavity networks that may become through-paths after machining, especially between machined surfaces and in thread-rolled internal bores. In thin-walled or high-quality gas-tight castings, narrow connected pores and bottlenecks are particularly important: flow resistance rises sharply as the channel radius decreases, so small cross-sections near the surface can prevent adequate evacuation and resin penetration. Vacuum impregnation can seal interconnected porosity when the cavity network is accessible and sufficiently permeable. Laboratory results cited state that pores below 100 μm are always saturated and cavities below 500 μm are generally likely to fill, but narrow entrances, contamination, or plastic deformation from machining and thread rolling can inhibit vacuuming and saturation. Even a 50–150 μm-long restriction with a diameter of only a few microns may drastically reduce impregnation effectiveness. Thus, impregnation is a viable remedial or production process, but it cannot reliably seal every connected leak path, particularly those with constricted surface outlets or deformation-induced bottlenecks.

## pqac-00000042

From text 'meng2008thepreparationof pages 56-61'.

DT MEng. The preparation of titanium alloys and composites via non melt processing. Unknown journal, 2008.

The excerpt describes HIP powder encapsulation in welded mild-steel cans; it does not provide an aluminium-can procedure. Cans, lids, and degassing tubes were machined from EN1A mild steel and assembled by TIG welding under Ar-30%He. The degassing tube was first welded to the lid, the bottom was welded to the can body, and titanium powder was poured into the open can. The powder was repeatedly tapped to settle it, initially leaving about 2 cm of clearance so the lid could be welded without heating nearby powder. After lid welding, additional powder was introduced through the degassing tube and the can was tapped until completely filled. The can was placed vertically in a tube furnace, with water cooling around the degassing tube to protect the vacuum-pump connection. Evacuation was performed using rotary and/or diffusion pumps. Once pressure stabilized at approximately 10^-1 mbar, high-purity argon was introduced and reflowed over the powder three times to displace oxygen; the gas was passed through silica gel and heated titanium turnings to reduce moisture and oxygen. Degassing then proceeded while heating at either 3 or 25°C/min to the selected temperature under vacuum. After degassing, the can was removed, the tube heated with an oxy-acetylene torch, and a hydraulic ram compressed the crimp. The tube was crimped twice, the lower crimp bent 90 degrees, and the excess tube cut away to seal the can.
